title: Big Bang Evidence: CMB and Beyond
welcome_lead: Hear the 2.7 K hiss of the cosmic microwave background and count primordial elements.

final_note: Three independent pillars: expansion, CMB and light-element abundances.

walkthroughs.body_html: Hot photons from 380,000 years after Big Bang have been redshifted to microwave wavelengths. Black body at 2.725 K, nearly uniform — a smoking gun for the Big Bang.
Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts ~75% H, ~25% He, trace Li by mass. Observations of pristine clouds match remarkably — strong support for hot early universe.
1) Hubble expansion. 2) CMB at 2.7 K. 3) Primordial light-element abundances. Together they make Big Bang the consensus model.

Was the Big Bang an explosion of matter into pre-existing space?
options: The galaxies are turning red because they are getting older.
Yes — it was a giant explosion at a point, and galaxies are still flying outwards from it.
No — it was the expansion of space itself, beginning from a hot dense state; there was no 'outside' for matter to expand into.
Yes — it was a bomb-like event that destroyed an earlier universe.

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological redshift of distant galaxies indicate?
options: The galaxies are turning red because they are getting older.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
Space itself is expanding, stretching the wavelength of light from distant galaxies as it travels.
Galaxies are moving through space away from us, like objects flying outward from a centre.

mcqs.q: Does Hooke's law apply to a spring for any amount of stretching?
options: Yes — it was a bomb-like event that destroyed an earlier universe.
Yes — Hooke's law applies to any spring at any extension.
No — it only holds up to the limit of proportionality; beyond that the relationship between force and extension is no longer linear.
Only when the force is small enough to be ignored.
